label: Title
notes: Open the lecture by naming the chapter as a certificate problem. A regular surface is not just a smooth-looking picture; the job is to prove that local coordinates, tangent planes, measurements, area, and normals behave consistently around every point.

label: Route
notes: Use the route slide as a dependency graph. Rank and regular-value tests create local models, chart changes make the model independent of notation, tangent planes support differentials, the first fundamental form measures vectors, and orientation asks whether local normal choices glue globally.

label: Patch Certificates
notes: Stress that a parametrization is only a surface chart where its two velocity vectors are independent. The cross product is the visible diagnostic in R3: when it vanishes, the coordinate grid has collapsed and no tangent plane has been certified.

label: Regular Values
notes: Compare the patch certificate with the implicit certificate. A level set F equals c becomes a surface when the gradient does not vanish on that level, because the gradient supplies a normal direction and the implicit function theorem supplies local coordinates.

label: Chart Changes
notes: Coordinate changes are the honesty test for a surface atlas. If two charts describe the same patch of surface, the transition map must be differentiable with an invertible Jacobian, so computations made in one coordinate system can be translated to the other.

label: Surface Functions
notes: A function on a surface is differentiable when it becomes a differentiable ordinary function after composing with every chart. The point is not to privilege a chart, but to make sure the function has the same differentiability status in all compatible coordinates.

label: Tangent Planes
notes: Present the tangent plane in its two equivalent languages. In coordinates it is spanned by x_u and x_v; intrinsically it is the set of velocities of curves on the surface through the point. The equivalence is what lets geometric arguments and coordinate computations talk to each other.

label: Differentials
notes: Frame the differential as the linear map seen by first-order observers riding on curves. If a surface map sends alpha on S to beta on S prime, then the derivative sends alpha prime at zero to beta prime at zero, and the definition must be independent of the chosen curve.

label: First Fundamental Form
notes: The first fundamental form is the imported dot product on each tangent plane. In a chart it becomes a symmetric matrix with entries E, F, and G, and this matrix is the local machine for lengths, angles, orthogonality, and area density.

label: Metric Ellipse
notes: Use the ellipse as a visual audit of anisotropic stretching. Unit coordinate vectors do not usually remain unit on the surface; the metric ellipse records which tangent directions are stretched more strongly and which directions are closer to orthogonal.

label: Area Density
notes: Move from measurement of vectors to measurement of patches. The density square root of EG minus F squared is the norm of x_u cross x_v, so the area formula is the same rank certificate integrated over a region with metric scale included.

label: Orientation
notes: Orientation is a global compatibility question, not a local existence question. Every regular patch gives a local normal, but an orientable surface allows those choices to be made coherently across overlaps so that walking around loops does not reverse the chosen normal.

label: Compact Oriented Surfaces
notes: Connect orientation to integral bookkeeping. On a compact oriented surface, consistent normal choices let local area elements be assembled without sign ambiguity. When a boundary is present, that normal choice also fixes the positive direction used along the boundary.

label: Helicoid Lab
notes: Use the helicoid as the applied laboratory because all chapter concepts are visible at once. The parametrization has a rank certificate, its first fundamental form is explicit, the area density grows with radius and pitch, and orientation is supplied by the normalized cross product.

label: Failure Modes
notes: Make the warning slide practical. Most mistakes in this chapter come from treating a drawing as a proof, using a single chart as if it were global, pushing tangent vectors without checking chart independence, or integrating area as though coordinates were already physical distances.

label: Recap
notes: Close by asking students to retain the certificate chain. Rank creates surface charts, compatible transitions create an atlas, tangent planes support differentials, the metric measures, the determinant integrates, and orientation glues local normal choices into a global decision.
